Dagster contributor: TaskFlow superficially looks like Dagster's APIs but differs - built on XCom not designed for large data, and using it loses Python dependency isolation between DAGs that Kubernetes Operators provide.

Dagster natively isolates tasks in the DAG into separate Kubernetes pods, unlike Airflow's CeleryExecutor (KubernetesExecutor only in Astronomer's Hybrid-SAAS). Dagster's local development is reportedly lighter weight and delightful.
One advantage Airflow has over Dagster is maturity and pre-built integrations - providers exist for Fivetran, Hightouch, Snowflake etc., which Dagster lacks in comparable breadth.

Dagster and Prefect won't ever have a hosted version on AWS/GCP consoles the way Airflow does, and large existing Airflow shops with big DE teams can't easily move to Dagster even if it has more features.

Asking a data analyst to write Python code to schedule SQL queries in Dagster still adds a barrier to entry, though Dagster is 'hitting the right chord' by focusing on Airflow's DX pain points, dev branches, and asset-based abstractions.

For anyone who has spent significant time with data and ML pipelines, read posts about Dagster... The software itself has matured significantly in the last year as well - highly recommend taking a look at this.
After playing around with this tool a bit in the past I can't seem to understand what it's trying to solve. It comes across as a side project that VCs happened to throw money at.

Dagster team member: goals are (1) local development seamless from laptop to CI to prod, (2) managing complexity of hundreds of DAGs/thousands of tasks, and (3) testability by separating business logic from environmental concerns unlike Airflow's hardcoded operators like EmrAddStepsOperator.

Blog authors report running the Dagster+dbt+DuckDB stack in production for months; it has downsides due to the young ecosystem (e.g., warehouse separation of storage/compute, metastore limitations) but also upsides for developer productivity.
Debugging Dagster can be a bit annoying; a blog post on interactive Dagster debugging was cited as the most helpful resource found.
